Eight Midwestern states received approval from EPA to remove the 1- pound-per-square-inch Reid vapor pressure waiver for summer gasoline containing E10, allowing for year-round sales effective April 28, 2025.13 2.7.1 Production, Consumption, and Capacity Most ethanol is produced using dry-mill technology (92%); a small number of larger plants use a wet-milling process (8%) (RFA 2025b). Dry milling is a process that grinds corn grain into flour and ferments only the starch component into ethanol with coproducts of distillers grains (an animal feed coproduct) and carbon dioxide. Wet-mill plants primarily produce corn grain sweeteners, along with ethanol and several other coproducts (such as corn oil and starch). Figure 23 highlights 2024 ethanol production and consumption of more than 16 billion gallons and 14 billion gallons, respectively (EIA 2025j). Exports account for the difference in production and consumption. Figure 24 shows cellulosic ethanol production including a large increase in 2024, a result of EPA using a new ASTM test method to quantify the pre- and post-fermentation cellulosic content (Primrose 2025). Since 2021, all cellulosic ethanol production is from bolt-on technology at existing conventional ethanol plants, which extracts the corn fiber byproduct for processing into ethanol. Adding cellulosic ethanol conversion technology to existing corn ethanol plants allows these facilities to diversify their portfolios. As of January 2025, there were 191 fuel ethanol plants with an installed capacity of about 18.5 billion gallons (Figure 25 and Figure 26). There are plants in 21 states, with the majority in the Midwest (Figure 18) (EIA 2025d). Plant ownership is not consolidated—there are approximately 114 ownership organizations.
